title: Suffering as a Christian: Stewards of Grace in the Last Days
summary: Because Christ suffered in the body, believers are to arm themselves with the same resolve and no longer live for the passions that once ruled them, even when former friends mock them for it. With the end of all things near, they must be sober, pray, love deeply, show hospitality, and use their gifts to serve one another. They should not be surprised by the fiery trial, but rejoice to share Christ's sufferings, never be ashamed to suffer as Christians, and entrust themselves to their faithful Creator.
story: Chapter 3 ended with Christ enthroned at God's right hand after suffering, with every power subject to him. Chapter 4 draws the consequence: those united to him must live the rest of their lives for God's will, even at a social cost. The first half (verses 1-11) finishes the letter's long section on living among unbelievers with a burst of community instructions and a doxology. The second half (verses 12-19) returns to suffering with new intensity, calling it a fiery trial and setting it in the light of the coming judgment, which begins with God's own household.
historical:
Verse 16 contains one of only three uses of the name Christian in the New Testament. According to Acts 11:26 the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch, and Agrippa uses the word in Acts 26:28. It was probably coined by outsiders, meaning partisans of Christ, and it could be used as a label of contempt. Within a few decades the name itself could bring legal danger. The Roman historian Tacitus reports that Nero blamed the Christians for the great fire of Rome in AD 64 and had many put to death. Around AD 110 to 112 Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia and Pontus (two of the regions addressed in this letter), wrote to the emperor Trajan asking whether people should be punished for the name alone, and Trajan's reply shows that confessing to be a Christian was treated as a punishable offense, though governors were not to hunt Christians out.

Peter's language of a fiery trial does not in itself show which of these settings the letter reflects. Scholars who date the letter to the early 60s read it as local hostility intensifying toward the Neronian violence; those who date it later see closer parallels to the situation Pliny describes. Either way, the readers were suffering reproach, abuse, and possible legal accusation simply for bearing Christ's name.
cultural:
The list of vices in verse 3 describes common features of social life in Greco-Roman towns: drinking parties, sexual license, and above all the banquets and festivals held in honor of the gods, which were also the main occasions for civic belonging, business networking, and trade guild fellowship. A convert who stopped attending looked strange and ungrateful, even disloyal to the city and its protecting gods, and former friends responded with abuse. Peter's reference to the dead in verse 5 and 6 may also answer the mockery that Christians' hope was empty because believers still died.

Hospitality was essential to the early church. Believers traveled for business and ministry, inns were unsafe or disreputable, and churches met in homes, so opening one's house was a constant, costly service, which is why Peter adds “without complaining”. A steward (oikonomos) was a household manager, often a trusted slave, who administered the master's resources on his behalf. Calling believers stewards of God's varied grace means their gifts belong to God and are held in trust for others.
literary: The chapter has two sections, each ending in praise to God. Verses 1-6 draw a contrast between life for human passions and life for God's will, rooted in Christ's suffering and the coming judgment. Verses 7-11 are introduced by the declaration “The end of all things is near” and give a compact set of community commands (prayer, love, hospitality, gifts for speaking and serving), ending with a doxology and Amen. Verses 12-19 begin with “Beloved”, as in 2:11, and return to suffering with the language of fire, sharing, glory, and judgment, ending with a quotation from Proverbs 11:31 (in its Greek form) and a final call to entrust oneself to God. The repeated contrast between suffering as a wrongdoer and suffering as a Christian echoes 2:20 and 3:17.

outline.t: Done with the old life, living for God's will
Love, hospitality, and gifts in the last days
Judgment begins with God's household; entrusting our souls to the Creator

doctrines.note: Believers should not be surprised by suffering for Christ, but rejoice to share in his sufferings, knowing that “the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you.” Suffering according to God's will is met by entrusting oneself to a faithful Creator and continuing to do good. That trust is not meant to be carried alone: the same chapter surrounds sufferers with a praying, hospitable church, and anyone overwhelmed should reach out to trusted people and, in danger, to emergency help.

Each believer has received a gift to use in serving others, as a steward of God's grace. Some serve with speech, others with practical service, and all for the purpose “that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.”

Christ “is ready to judge the living and the dead.” Judgment begins with the family of God, which here likely means refining discipline through suffering, and Peter uses it to show how serious the outcome will be for those who refuse the gospel.
Holiness is shown in a decisive break with the old life, sobriety, prayer, and deep love that “covers over a multitude of sins”, echoing Proverbs 10:12.

words.note: Christianos, Christian, a follower or partisan of Christ. The word appears only three times in the New Testament (Acts 11:26; 26:28; here). Peter turns a label that could be used in contempt into a name to bear without shame, since to suffer for it is to glorify God.

Purōsis, burning or fiery ordeal. The word recalls the refining fire of 1:7, where faith is tested like gold. The fiery trial is painful but not strange, and it serves to prove and purify faith rather than destroy it.

Oikonomos, steward or household manager, the person who administered a household's resources for its owner. Peter calls believers stewards of God's manifold grace: every gift is God's property, entrusted for the good of others.

Charisma, a gift of grace. Paul uses the same word for spiritual gifts in Romans 12 and 1 Corinthians 12. Peter groups gifts into two broad kinds, speaking and serving, and insists that each be exercised in God's strength and for his glory.

christ: Christ's suffering in the body is the ground of the chapter's call to holy living (verse 1), and Christ is the one ready to judge the living and the dead (verse 5), a role the New Testament consistently gives him (Acts 10:42; 2 Timothy 4:1). Believers share in his sufferings now so that they may rejoice at the revelation of his glory, a union with Christ so close that insults aimed at his name land on them, and the Spirit of glory rests on them. Every gift is exercised so that God may be glorified “through Jesus Christ”, and the doxology gives him glory and power forever. To bear the name Christian is to be known by his name, which Peter treats as an honor worth suffering for.

hard.q: Verse 6 says the gospel was preached even to the dead. Does this mean people can hear the gospel after death?
hard.a:
Interpreters read verse 6 in two main ways. Many take it to mean that the gospel was preached to believers during their lifetimes who have since died. Pagan neighbors may have mocked that Christians die like everyone else, and Peter answers that though they were judged in the flesh (they died, perhaps even under condemnation by others), they will live before God in the spirit. The word now in the BSB's “those who are now dead” reflects this reading, which fits the immediate context of verse 5 and the letter's concern with judgment.

Others connect the verse with 3:19 and read it as Christ's proclamation to the dead between his death and resurrection, and some in the early church and later drew from this a hope that those who died without hearing the gospel might hear it. Most Christian traditions have been cautious about building a doctrine of a second chance after death on this verse, given Hebrews 9:27 and the uncertainty of its meaning, but they differ over what hope may be held for those who never heard. Peter's own point is pastoral: death does not defeat the gospel, and those who suffered for Christ are not lost.

questions: Peter's readers lost friends and social standing by refusing old ways of life. What has following Christ cost you socially, and how does this chapter speak to that?
What gift has God entrusted to you as a steward, and who is it meant to serve?
Verse 19 tells sufferers to entrust their souls to a faithful Creator and keep doing good. What would that look like in a painful situation you are facing?
